title: Using Python MockServer for API Testing
summary: Use Python requests with MockServer’s REST API to create expectations, test failure responses, verify calls, and reset state between tests.
body_markdown:
A mock server lets a Python application exercise its real HTTP client without calling the real dependency. You control the response, then check that the application sent the expected request and handled the result.


[MockServer](https://www.mock-server.com/) runs as a separate service. Python is the client in this walkthrough. The examples use` requests` to call MockServer’s REST API directly, so they do not depend on an additional Python wrapper or an assumed` client.expect` interface.


## Start a disposable MockServer


With Docker running, start a local instance:


```text
docker   run   -d   --rm   --name   python-mockserver-demo   \
-p   127.0.0.1:1080:1080   mockserver/mockserver:5.15.0
```


This walkthrough pins 5.15.0 to keep its example reproducible; it is not a claim that this is the latest release. For other deployment methods and versions, use the[MockServer running guide](https://www.mock-server.com/mock_server/running_mock_server.html) .


Wait until MockServer is ready:


```text
curl   -i   -X   PUT   http://127.0.0.1:1080/mockserver/status
```


A successful status response shows the server is reachable. If port 1080 is occupied, choose another host port and update the base URL in every example.


Create a Python virtual environment and install the HTTP client:


```text
python3   -m   venv   .venv
source   .venv/bin/activate
python   -m   pip   install   requests
```


## Create an expectation and exercise it


Save this as` mockserver_demo.py` . It clears the dedicated demo instance, registers a GET response, calls it, and checks the result.


```text
import   requests


BASE_URL   =   "http://127.0.0.1:1080"


def   reset  ():
response   =   requests.put(  f  "  {BASE_URL}  /mockserver/reset"  ,   timeout  =  5  )
response.raise_for_status()


def   expect  (request, response):
result   =   requests.put(
f  "  {BASE_URL}  /mockserver/expectation"  ,
json  =  {  "httpRequest"  : request,   "httpResponse"  : response},
timeout  =  5  ,
)
result.raise_for_status()


reset()
expect(
{  "method"  :   "GET"  ,   "path"  :   "/api/example"  },
{
"statusCode"  :   200  ,
"headers"  : {  "Content-Type"  : [  "application/json"  ]},
"body"  :   '{"message": "Hello, MockServer!"}'  ,
},
)


response   =   requests.get(  f  "  {BASE_URL}  /api/example"  ,   timeout  =  5  )
assert   response.status_code   ==   200
assert   response.json()   ==   {  "message"  :   "Hello, MockServer!"  }
print  (  "GET expectation passed"  )
```


Run it with` python mockserver_demo.py` . MockServer’s[expectation documentation](https://www.mock-server.com/mock_server/creating_expectations.html) describes the` httpRequest` matcher and the` httpResponse` action used here.


In an application test, configure the application’s dependency base URL to point at MockServer, then exercise the application instead of calling the mock directly. A direct request checks the fixture; a request through the application checks its client and error handling.


## Test an error response


Append this block to the same file. Resetting first removes the earlier expectation, so the result does not depend on expectation ordering.


```text
reset()
request   =   {
"method"  :   "POST"  ,
"path"  :   "/external/api"  ,
"body"  : {  "type"  :   "JSON"  ,   "json"  :   '{"key": "value"}'  },
}
expect(
request,
{
"statusCode"  :   502  ,
"headers"  : {  "Content-Type"  : [  "application/json"  ]},
"body"  :   '{"error": "Bad Gateway"}'  ,
},
)


response   =   requests.post(
f  "  {BASE_URL}  /external/api"  ,   json  =  {  "key"  :   "value"  },   timeout  =  5
)
assert   response.status_code   ==   502
assert   response.json()[  "error"  ]   ==   "Bad Gateway"
print  (  "Error expectation passed"  )
```


When testing your application, assert on its observable behavior: a bounded retry count, the documented fallback, or the error returned to its caller. Receiving the configured 502 from MockServer alone does not establish those behaviors.


## Verify that the request was received


A configured response does not prove the application used it. Append a verification request after the POST:


```text
verification   =   requests.put(
f  "  {BASE_URL}  /mockserver/verify"  ,
json  =  {
"httpRequest"  : request,
"times"  : {  "atLeast"  :   1  ,   "atMost"  :   1  },
},
timeout  =  5  ,
)
verification.raise_for_status()
print  (  "Exactly one matching POST was received"  )
```


The[verification API](https://www.mock-server.com/mock_server/verification.html) checks recorded requests. Match the fields that matter to the behavior you are testing rather than every incidental header.


## Test a timeout and clean up


Append a delayed response and use a shorter client timeout:


```text
reset()
expect(
{  "method"  :   "GET"  ,   "path"  :   "/delayed/response"  },
{
"statusCode"  :   200  ,
"body"  :   "delayed"  ,
"delay"  : {  "timeUnit"  :   "SECONDS"  ,   "value"  :   2  },
},
)


try  :
requests.get(  f  "  {BASE_URL}  /delayed/response"  ,   timeout  =  0.2  )
except   requests.exceptions.ReadTimeout:
print  (  "Client timed out as expected"  )
else  :
raise   AssertionError  (  "Expected a read timeout"  )
finally  :
reset()
```


The[reset endpoint](https://www.mock-server.com/mock_server/clearing_and_resetting.html) clears expectations and recorded requests. Use it only on a dedicated test instance; resetting a shared server can break another test. Give parallel tests separate instances or coordinate their state explicitly.


Stop the demo container when finished:


```text
docker   stop   python-mockserver-demo
```


## When to use recorded mocks


Handwritten expectations work well when a test needs a small, explicit scenario. They still encode your assumptions about the dependency. MockServer also has[record-and-replay support](https://www.mock-server.com/proxy/record_and_replay.html) , so recording is not exclusive to Speedscale.


If you want a workflow built around recording supported application traffic and reusing it as mocks and regression tests, start with the[proxymock local guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/quickstart/local/) . The[mocking tools comparison](https://speedscale.com/blog/api-mocking-tools/) can help you choose the boundary. Keep real-service integration checks for authentication, provider behavior, and contracts that your fixtures cannot establish.
